source.title: Super Suffixes: Bypassing Text Generation Alignment and Guard Models Simultaneously
source.authors: Andrew Adiletta; Kathryn Adiletta; Kemal Derya; B. Sunar

record.tranche_reason: The study extracts a difference-in-means refusal direction and uses suffix optimization targeting that direction, then reports refusal rates. It does not perform the original direct activation ablation or addition.
record.gate_note: The study reports refusal rates for prompts with no suffix, a primary suffix optimized against the refusal direction, and a jointly optimized Super Suffix. These bear on direction-targeted suppression and refusal behavior. Guard benign-probability scores and DeltaGuard classification results concern guard evasion or detection, not the claim versions' refusal behavior, so they are not rows. Direction/layer selection counts in Table 2 and concept-direction similarities used for analysis are not rows because they are used to choose or characterize the method.
record.test_reason: The study uses an Arditi-style difference-in-means refusal direction as a loss term for an IRIS-like suffix attack and a DeltaGuard detector. It reports only its own attack's success and the guard's evasion. There is no ablation, no addition, no non-direction GCG control, and no test of whether refusal is mediated by the direction. The suffixes are optimized to suppress the direction, so the refusal drops show the method works, not that V1 or V3 holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that jointly optimized Super Suffixes break generator alignment and evade Llama Prompt Guard 2 across five models, on HarmBench and a new malicious-code dataset. They also find that adding the secondary suffix slightly weakens the attack on the generator. DeltaGuard, a KNN on refusal-direction cosine traces, raises non-benign classification of these attacks to near 100%.
record.recipe_differences: The study constructs difference-in-means concept directions and optimizes suffixes to reduce activations along a refusal direction, but does not directly ablate or add that direction in activations or weights.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with prompt set and suffix type: Super Suffixes leave more refusals than primary suffixes, and HarmBench results are weaker or reversed in some cases compared with malicious code-generation prompts. The authors also report that direction and target layer choices affect primary-suffix success.

fits_no_version.finding: Cosine-similarity traces to the refusal direction (Fig. 4, Gemma 2B) differ between malicious, benign, primary-suffix and Super Suffix prompts around output start. A KNN on these traces (DeltaGuard) detects suffixed prompts with benign probability at most 0.07.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Temporal refusal-direction similarity traces distinguish jailbreak-suffixed prompts from benign and plainly malicious ones (detection use of the direction).

fits_no_version.finding: On Llama3.2 3B, primary-suffix success depends strongly on the extraction and target layer: 27/29 for direction 13 / layer 15 versus 2–11/29 for other pairs (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Direction-targeted suffix attacks are sensitive to which layer's refusal direction is used.

record.code_released: The authors state that code and data will be made available pending internal review; no release URL is stated.
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. There is no direct activation ablation or addition and no general-capability evaluation. The study uses a particular suffix-optimization attack as an indirect test of direction-mediated refusal. The text describes Vicuna's no-suffix malicious-code refusal rate as 37%, while Table 3 reports 0.35.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2's primary-suffix success counts by direction/layer are used to select settings, so they are omitted. Table 6 and related DeltaGuard results measure guard classification rather than refusal behavior. Concept-direction token lists and cosine-similarity plots are not reported as outcomes on a claim version.

untested.parts: Ablation, addition, and capability preservation are not performed; the direction is only used as an attack loss.
No independent jailbreak is analysed for direction suppression, and no robustness training; the attacks are built to suppress the direction.

record.verdict_notes: Records the reader's V1/V3 labels are dropped: the refusal rates measure the study's own attack, which is optimized to suppress the direction and selected through iterative search, with no ablation or non-direction baseline. Source inconsistencies: Vicuna no-suffix code refusal is 37% in the text vs 0.35 in Table 3. The HarmBench text says Vicuna 'dropped to 20%', but Table 4 shows Vicuna at 0.76 and Llama3.1 at 0.20. No uncertainty is reported; this is a preprint.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not directly project the direction out of every layer and position, add the direction to induce refusals, or measure whether general capabilities remain intact. Its intervention is a direction-targeted suffix, not direct activation ablation.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is performed.
The study tests direction-targeted suffix attacks and their effects on refusal, but does not test training against the ablation or measure robustness after such training.
The study does not test whether refusal is better represented by an affine subspace, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
No separate harmfulness-judgment representation and refusal-decision representation are tested.
Models are tested separately; transfer of a direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models is not tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or timing is conducted.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Primary suffixes on malicious code-generation prompts for the five tested models
reader_labels.reason: The direction-targeted suffix reduces refusal in the reported model settings, including to 0.00 for Vicuna; this is indirect support from suffix optimization rather than direct activation ablation (r2, r5, r8, r11, r14).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Refusal remains appreciable for Super Suffixes and many HarmBench primary-suffix settings, with an increase rather than a decrease for Vicuna on HarmBench; direct ablation, addition, and capability preservation are not tested (r3, r6, r9, r12, r15, r17, r18, r20, r21, r23, r24, r26, r27, r29, r30).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Primary suffix attacks on malicious code-generation prompts
reader_labels.reason: Suffixes optimized against the refusal direction substantially lower refusal rates across all five models in this dataset (r2, r5, r8, r11, r14).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: HarmBench primary suffixes and Super Suffixes
reader_labels.reason: The effect varies by dataset and suffix: some HarmBench refusal rates remain high, Vicuna's HarmBench refusal rate rises, and Super Suffixes generally leave more refusals than primary suffixes (r17, r18, r20, r21, r23, r24, r26, r27, r29, r30). The training-robustness part is untested.
